articles.title: Skip Bayless subtly mentions 11-year-old LeBron James tweet while praising 76ers star vs Knicks
articles.summary: LeBron James starred for the Philadelphia 76ers in their 98-93 win over the New York Knicks in the NBA Cup. The Sixers have had a fine start to the campaign,...
articles.body:
LeBron James starred for the Philadelphia 76ers in their 98-93 win over the New York Knicks in the NBA Cup.

The Sixers have had a fine start to the campaign, and they continued their regular-season form in the Cup by picking up another impressive win over the Knicks.

James arguably had his best game in a 76ers' shirt, so much so that even Skip Bayless has praised him.

Skip Bayless brings back LeBron James' 'fit in and not fit out' quote to praise him

Tyrese Maxey was probably the best player in the game, having scored a game-high 27 points along with four rebounds and four assists.

However, as always, all eyes were on James to see what he could do, and The King did not disappoint.

James recorded 20 points, nine rebounds and eight assists in what was a fantastic performance for the 76ers against the Knicks.

After the game, Bayless reacted by saying on X: "Sixers continue to show they're just better than the champs. Held Knicks to 93.

"No JB, but LeBron had a strong game: 20/9/8, nice lane fadeaway with 1:10 left and a late follow. He's fitting in, not out."

Eagle-eyed James fans would immediately recognise that the last five words from Bayless' tweet are actually from one of LeBron's posts over 11 years ago.

Back in 2015, the then-Cavaliers superstar tweeted : "Stop trying to find a way to FIT-OUT and just FIT-IN. Be a part of something special! Just my thoughts."

James' post at the time was said to be a subliminal jab directed at his then-Cleveland Cavaliers teammate Kevin Love, who had spoken out about trying to 'fit out' rather than 'fit in' with the team.

Fast-forward 11 years, James is definitely fitting in with the 76ers, and that has helped them win all but one game so far this season.

articles.title: Stephen Curry breaks Luka Dončić's ankles as part of 25-point comeback in NBA Cup win
articles.summary: The Warriors trailed by 25. They won by 17 points. No NBA team had ever done that in the play-by-play era.
articles.body:
Luka Dončić's was ready to make a statement in the Los Angeles Lakers' NBA Cup opener on Friday. It worked, for a single quarter.

The Lakers opened the game on a 40-15 run that extended into the second quarter, with the Golden State Warriors once again looking like a deteriorating roster. Dončić appeared to be on a mission in particular, posting 25 points, 5 assists, 3 rebounds and 2 steals in the first quarter alone.

That might have had something to do with his previous run-in with Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg . Regardless, the rest of the game didn't work out so well for Los Angeles.

By halftime, the game was tied after the Warriors went on a 40-15 run over the course of 11 minutes and 39 seconds. By the third quarter, they led by five. About four minutes into the fourth quarter, they led by 16.

The game ultimately went down as a 112-95 Warriors win, with Stephen Curry posting the highlight by dropping Dončić in the third quarter before a 3-pointer to cut the deficit to six.

In fairness, Dončić responded with his own 3-pointer, which wasn't enough to avoid some unfortunate history. Per Keerthika Uthayakuma r , the 17-point margin of victory is the largest ever posted by a team that had trailed by 25 points in the same game in the play-by-play era (since 1996).

Curry finished the game with 31 points on 11-of-23 shooting (8-of-14 from 3-point range) plus 6 assists and 4 rebounds. That scoring total was enough to push him up to No. 18 on the NBA's all-time scoring leaderboard, passing Dominique Wilkins.

Dončić, meanwhile, had 37 points on 12-of-27 shooting, 7 rebounds and 5 assists. That continues a torrid pace for the Lakers star to begin the season.

The Warriors have posted three straight wins after opening the season 0-3 for the first time since drafting Curry , with their other wins coming against the Denver Nuggets and Minnesota Timberwolves. This win, and the record margin of victory, also gives them a significant leg up in NBA Cup play, where they share a group with the Lakers, San Antonio Spurs, Portland Trail Blazers and Sacramento Kings.

articles.title: Lakers blow 25-point lead in double-digit loss to Warriors
articles.summary: The Lakers take a 21-point lead in the first quarter and build it to 25 before the Warriors race back to tie the score at halftime and win the second-half ba...
articles.body:
When Luka Doncic started cooking in the first quarter, the Lakers followed his lead in opening a 25-point lead in the second quarter over the Golden State Warriors on Friday night.

But then the Lakers started getting cooked.

Cooked by going down by 17 points in the fourth quarter. Cooked by turning the ball over way too many times. Cooked by an offense nowhere to be found in the fourth. Cooked in the first NBA Cup game for both teams.

When the game was over, the Lakers had been feasted on by the Warriors, falling 112-95 game at Chase Center.

Doncic had 37 points, but he shot only 12 for 27 from the field. Austin Reaves had 21 points, shooting nine for 19 from the field but one of six from three-point range.

For the Warriors, Stephen Curry had 31 points, going 11 for 23 from the field and eight for 14 from deep.

The Lakers scored only 15 points in the fourth quarter and gave up 27.

It took the Lakers four minutes and one second to finally score in the fourth quarter, and that came after Walker Kessler made just one free throw with 7:54 left in the game, leaving the Lakers down 96-81.

The Lakers showed why they are one of the worst teams in the NBA when taking care of the basketball by turning it over 22 times. They are ranked 10th in the NBA in turnovers, averaging 16.6 per game.

After Jake LaRavia was called for an offensive foul with 21.8 seconds left in the third quarter, Doncic was hit with his first technical foul of the season.

But Doncic really wasn't the only Laker to lose his cool. The Lakers turned the ball over five times in the third and wound up trailing 85-80 entering the fourth quarter.

With 8:02 left in the fourth and the Lakers down 95-80, Matisse Thybulle was hit with a technical foul and Curry made the ensuing free throw.

The Lakers went to sleep in the second quarter and started to get cooked by the Warriors, watching their big lead get sliced to 53-53 at the half.

The Lakers were outscored 38-15 in the second quarter. Interesting enough, the Lakers outscored the Warriors 38-15 in the first quarter.

Curry crossed over Doncic, sending him falling on the court in the third quarter. Curry then made a three-pointer and put his hands on his head.

Doncic came right back, drilling a three-pointer over Gary Payton II on the next possession and put his fingers on his lips and glared at the crowd.

On the Lakers' first possession of the game, Doncic got the ball at the top of the key, and he was being guarded by his new antagonist, Golden State's brash rookie Yaxel Lendeborg.

Doncic missed his first shot, a floater. The Lakers got the ball back on the miss and the Warriors fans began to chant, "Luka, sucks. Luka sucks, Luka sucks."

Doncic responded by knocking down a three-pointer in the face of Lendeborg, and then wagged his finger at his would-be defender.

Doncic and Lendeborg began a trash-talking exchange when the Lakers and Warriors opened the season against each other last week.

After that game, in which Doncic posted 41 points and nine assists, Lendeborg was not impressed by the Lakers' scoring sensation, saying he "lost all respect" for Doncic.

But as he so often does, Doncic went to work in the first quarter, terrorizing Lendeborg and the Warriors' faithful with 21 points. He missed just five of his 12 shots and four of his nine-three-pointers in the opening 12 minutes.

Before the game, Lakers coach JJ Redick was asked what it has been like to see Doncic respond when the opposition "pokes the bear," as Lendeborg did in Los Angeles.

"I mean, he's insane," Redick said. "He's involved in everything in every game so it doesn't like … I don't think that's like an anomaly. It's part of the Luka basketball game. I didn't view that as like an outlier at all."

Ziaire Williams missed his second straight game with left foot soreness. The starting forward has been one of the team's better defenders.

"He still has some soreness," Redick said. "He's going to have to continue to monitor it. He was in shootaround this morning. Again, just being really cautious with the amount of games we have throughout the season."

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Immediate takeaway. Suns go from 'terrible' to worse on defense
articles.summary: Here's an immediate takeaway from Phoenix Suns 127-120 loss Oct. 30 to Denver Nuggets in NBA Cup play.
articles.body:
The Phoenix Suns preached and stressed defense for three straight days – and for good reason.

They have the worst defensive ranking in the league.

Then, Phoenix came out and allowed the Denver Nuggets to shoot as high 70% from 3 at one point in its 127-120 loss in NBA Cup group play at Mortgage Matchup Center on Friday, Oct. 30.

The Nuggets (3-2) torched the Suns (1-3) for 61% shooting in the first half fueled by a 13-of-20 effort from 3.

Christian Braun came into the game shooting a career-low 23.8% from 3 this season. He was 2-of-13 from distance in Denver's first three games.

Braun sees the Suns and becomes Stephen Curry – 6-of-6 from 3 in the first half.

See photos from Suns' road matchup vs. Thunder

After one made 3, OK, all good. After two, OK, he might get it going.

After the third and fourth? Might want to get a hand in his face instead of leaving him bare in the short corner.

The Nuggets came into the game in the bottom third in offensive rating. They should climb those charts after blitzing Phoenix's defense.

The Suns have allowed at least 122 points in their four games, giving up a season-high Friday night before a sellout crowd of 17,071 that started leaving after Braun hit his seventh 3 late in the game in scoring a career-high 31 points.

Jamal Murray lit up the Suns for a game-high 39 points, hitting 7-of-9 from 3.

Stop all the point guard talk. Stop all the offense talk. The Suns have been atrocious on defense this season -- Dillon Brooks used the word 'terrible' earlier this week -- after finishing ninth in defensive ranking last season.

That's not digression. That's inexcusable.

articles.title: James, Maxey fuel 76ers over Knicks in NBA Cup thriller
articles.summary: LeBron James scored 20 points including a late tip-in to help seal the Philadelphia 76ers' 98-93 victory over the NBA champion New York Knicks on Friday.Jame...
articles.body:
LeBron James scored 20 points including a late tip-in to help seal the Philadelphia 76ers' 98-93 victory over the NBA champion New York Knicks on Friday.

The 76ers notched their second win of the young season over the Knicks after spoiling their championship banner-raising with a victory at Madison Square Garden on opening night.

The win had a double edge as Friday's games marked the start of the fourth edition of the NBA Cup, the NBA in-season tournament won by the Knicks before they went on to beat the San Antonio Spurs in the NBA Finals for their first championship since 1973.

Group-stage Cup games will be played throughout November, all counting in the regular-season standings. Quarter-finals will be played December 4-5 and semi-finals December 8-9 before the final on December 11 at Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Indiana.

Tyrese Maxey scored 27 points to lead the Sixers, who took control early against the sloppy Knicks.

They led by 14 in the third quarter and weathered a late Knicks surge.

Jalen Brunson's step-back three-pointer put New York up 90-89 with 1:32 remaining.

James, the NBA's all-time leading scorer, answered with a basket that put Philadelphia back in front and pushed the lead to 96-91 with a tip-in off a Maxey miss with 11.9 seconds left.

James, 41, added nine rebounds, eight assists, one steal and a vintage chase-down block in what 76ers coach Nick Nurse called his best game since joining as a free agent in June.

"I thought he was really good all the way through," Nurse said. "When we got some downhill stuff he used his size and knocked them around a little bit for some layups... kind of pushed and organized it.

"He's been good, but that was his best game, for sure."

Brunson led New York with 24 points and Karl-Anthony Towns added 22 points and 12 rebounds for the Knicks, who fell to 2-4.

The Dallas Mavericks, fueled by 35 points from Kyrie Irving and 33 from Cooper Flagg, rallied to hand the Houston Rockets their first defeat of the season 116-111.

The Rockets had emerged from a back-and-forth first half with a 51-44 lead, pushing the advantage to as many as 11 before taking an eight-point lead into the final frame.

Irving's three-pointer with 7:01 remaining put Dallas back in front and they wouldn't trail again, the Mavs finding an answer when Houston twice pulled level in the final stretch.

"It felt good," Irving said. "We came in at halftime, we weren't proud of our effort. We looked each other in the eye and we were just like, we've got to do better.

"We didn't bring it in the first half, but the second half we definitely brought it."

Golden State star Stephen Curry scored 31 points to lead the Warriors to a 112-95 victory over the Los Angeles Lakers in a rollercoaster contest in San Francisco.

The Lakers out-scored the Warriors 38-15 in the first quarter, the Warriors erasing the 23-point deficit by outscoring Los Angeles 38-15 in the second to knot it 53-53 at halftime.

Luka Doncic scored 37 points for the Lakers. The night's abiding image was of him crashing to the floor as he was wrong-footed by Curry -- who fired over him for a three-pointer.

Curry took his career points tally to 26,674, surpassing Dominique Wilkins (26,668) for 18th on the all-time scoring list.

In Miami, Giannis Antetokounmpo delivered a triple-double of 31 points, 18 rebounds and 10 assists to propel the Heat to a 145-125 victory over the Indiana Pacers.

In Boston, the Celtics romped to a 125-111 victory over the Chicago Bulls. Payton Pritchard scored 30 points off the bench and Jayson Tatum scored 26 for the Celtics, who led by as many as 32 points.

The Orlando Magic drained 18 three-pointers and withstood a career-high 41-point performance from Toronto's Scottie Barnes.

articles.title: LeBron James, Tyrese Maxey shine as 76ers beat Knicks in NBA Cup thriller
articles.summary: LeBron scored 20 points and hit the go-ahead fadeaway late, and Maxey had 27 points to lead the 76ers to a victory.
articles.body:
LeBron James scored 20 points, including a late tip-in, to help seal the Philadelphia 76ers’ 98-93 victory over the NBA champions New York Knicks on Friday.

The 76ers notched their second win of the young season over the Knicks after spoiling their championship banner-raising with a victory at Madison Square Garden on opening night.

The win had a double edge as Friday’s games marked the start of the fourth edition of the NBA Cup, the NBA in-season tournament won by the Knicks before they went on to beat the San Antonio Spurs in the NBA Finals for their first championship since 1973.

Group-stage Cup games will be played throughout November, all counting in the regular-season standings. Quarterfinals will be played December 4-5 and semifinals December 8-9 before the final on December 11 at Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Indiana.

Tyrese Maxey scored 27 points to lead the Sixers, who took control early against the sloppy Knicks.

They led by 14 in the third quarter and weathered a late Knicks surge.

Jalen Brunson’s step-back three-pointer put New York up 90-89 with 1:32 remaining.

James, the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, answered with a basket that put Philadelphia back in front and pushed the lead to 96-91 with a tip-in off a Maxey miss with 11.9 seconds left.

James, 41, added nine rebounds, eight assists, one steal and a vintage chase-down block in what 76ers coach Nick Nurse called his best game since joining as a free agent in July .

“I thought he was really good all the way through,” Nurse said. “When we got some downhill stuff, he used his size and knocked them around a little bit for some layups … kind of pushed and organised it.

“He’s been good, but that was his best game, for sure.”

Brunson led New York with 24 points, and Karl-Anthony Towns added 22 points and 12 rebounds for the Knicks, who fell to 2-4.

The Dallas Mavericks, fuelled by 35 points from Kyrie Irving and 33 from Cooper Flagg, rallied to hand the Houston Rockets their first defeat of the season, 116-111.

The Rockets had emerged from a back-and-forth first half with a 51-44 lead, pushing the advantage to as many as 11 before taking an eight-point lead into the final frame.

Irving’s three-pointer with 7:01 remaining put Dallas back in front, and they wouldn’t trail again, the Mavs finding an answer when Houston twice pulled level in the final stretch.

“It felt good,” Irving said. “We came in at halftime, we weren’t proud of our effort. We looked each other in the eye, and we were just like, we’ve got to do better.

“We didn’t bring it in the first half, but the second half we definitely brought it.”

Golden State star Stephen Curry scored 31 points to lead the Warriors to a 112-95 victory over the Los Angeles Lakers in a rollercoaster contest in San Francisco.

The Lakers outscored the Warriors 38-15 in the first quarter, the Warriors erasing the 23-point deficit by outscoring Los Angeles 38-15 in the second to knot it 53-53 at halftime.

Luka Doncic scored 37 points for the Lakers. The night’s abiding image was of him crashing to the floor as he was wrong-footed by Curry – who fired over him for a three-pointer.

Curry took his career points tally to 26,674, surpassing Dominique Wilkins (26,668) for 18th on the all-time scoring list.

In Miami, Giannis Antetokounmpo delivered a triple-double of 31 points, 18 rebounds and 10 assists to propel the Heat to a 145-125 victory over the Indiana Pacers.

In Boston, the Celtics romped to a 125-111 victory over the Chicago Bulls. Payton Pritchard scored 30 points off the bench, and Jayson Tatum scored 26 for the Celtics, who led by as many as 32 points.

Orlando’s Desmond Bane scored 28 points, Franz Wagner added 26 and Wendell Carter chipped in 20 as the Magic fended off a late challenge to beat the Raptors 121-114 in Toronto.

The Magic drained 18 three-pointers and withstood a career-high 41-point performance from Toronto’s Scottie Barnes.

Detroit shook off a slow start to hand the winless Nets a fifth straight defeat in Brooklyn, where Cade Cunningham scored 20 points, and Ron Holland added 18 off the bench in a 110-94 Pistons victory.

articles.title: Curry tumba a Doncic (literalmente) y comanda la histórica remontada de los Warriors
articles.standfirst: El equipo de San Francisco enjugó 25 puntos a los angelinos
articles.summary: El equipo de San Francisco enjugó 25 puntos a los angelinos
articles.body: Hay una jugada en este partido que prevalecerá sobre el resto y quizá sobre la mayoría de las que se produzcan a lo largo de la temporada. A 6:22 para el final del tercer cuatro con 60-69, Curry se mide a Doncic fuera del arco, lo reta, lo hace bailar y luego lo tumba en el suelo y lo acaba humillando con un triple sensacional, con el esloveno a sus pies. Es la jugada que resume el partido que los Warriors acabaron ganando, 112-95, a pesar de ir perdiendo por 25 puntos al final del primer cuarto. Curry es un mago que disfruta jugando. Y mientras sienta ese 'picorcito' seguirá siendo un jugador imparable. Ante los Lakers lideró una remontada de 25 puntos (15-40) para acabar ganando, dejando varias marcas por el camino. Los Lakers arrancaron con fuerza y se llevaron el primer cuarto, 15-38. Esa ventaja recortada por los Warriors se convirtió en la mayor remontada en la era del reloj de posesión de un equipo que perdía por 20 o más al final del primer cuarto. El 4 de marzo de 1976, los propios Warriors perdían 41-18 al final del primer acto y acabaron ganando. "Hay que decir que 25 puntos son los nuevos 12. Estamos viendo estas remontadas casi habitualmente", decía Steve Kerr, entrenador de los Warriors, al final del partido". Pero además con sus 31 puntos, Curry se ha convertido en el decimoctavo mejor anotador de todos los tiempos superando a una leyenda como Doiminique Wilkins (26.668). Luka Doncic dio una exhibición en el primer cuarto: 21 puntos con 7 de 12 en tiros (cinco triples), cinco asistencias y un par de robos. Acabó con 37 puntos y metido en la foto del partido. La derrota no fue culpa suya, aunque del 7/12 del primer cuarto se pasara al 5/14 del resto del partido. Curiosamente el 15-38 del primer cuarto a favor de los Lakers fue contestado por un 38-15 de los Warriors en el segundo acto para llegar al descanso igualados. Los Warriors no tuvieron que esperar mucho para remontar, su horrible salida de partido quedó neutralizada en un sólo periodo: 53-53. En ese momento, la afición de los Warriors gritaba 'Luka sucks' (Luka apesta). Los de San Francisco, que además tuvieron a Podziemski con 21, a Melton con 16 y a Niang con 11 (y tres titulares, Green, Santos y Lendeborg que apenas sumaron 10 entre los tres), cimentaron su triunfo en el 27-15 del último cuarto ya con Curry adueñado del partido. Anotó ocho puntos en el tercer acto y nueve en el cuarto. En los Lakers (11 de 39 en triples), además de Doncic estuvo bien Reaves, 21 y poco más. Entre los siete jugadores del banquillo, tann sólo aportaron siete puntos (Mamukelashvili 4 y Grimes 3), pero el georgiano, por ejemplo, acabó con un -23 en el +/- de su equipo.

articles.title: El mejor LeBron se vuelve a cargar a los campeones
articles.standfirst: Los Sixers, comandados por 'The King' y por Maxey, ganan por segunda vez a los New York Knicks
articles.summary: Los Sixers, comandados por 'The King' y por Maxey, ganan por segunda vez a los New York Knicks
articles.body: Cada vez que los Sixers y los Knicks se miden en el Este, viene a la mente 'Juego de Tronos'. Parece claro que ambos equipos se jugarán la corona de la conferencia para disputar las Finales, y Philadelphia ya lleva cierta ventaja. Y en parte, es culpa de LeBron James. 'The King' sacó su mejor versión y facilitó el triunfo de su equipo, 98-93, ante su público en el Xfinity Mobile Arena. No fue el máximo anotador de su equipo, pero sí el más decisivo, un papel que lleva 24 años desempeñando. Un 'stepback' fuera del arco de tres de Jalen Brunson heló el Xfinity Mobile Arena a 1:32 para el final, 89-90. Pero los Sixers tenían su respuesta: LeBron se fabricó la jugada delante de Anunoby para anotar con un 'fade away' en la siguiente posesión, a 1:10. Esa jugada llevó la tranquilidad a los Sixers: "LeBron es la calma cuando el partido se pone movido", dijo Maxey al final. Philly supo jugar mejor los últimos segundos, una vez más. Sus cinco triunfos han llegado en el tramo final. Llegaron un triple de Edgcombe y otra canasta de LeBron a 12 segundos para sellar el triunfo, 96-91. Los Sixers volvieron a tumbar a los campeones para seguir con ventaja en su particular 'Juego de Tronos' del Este. James acabó rozando el triple-doble con 20 puntos, nueve rebotes y nueve asistencias. Es su primer partido de 20 puntos con los Sixers y el 68 de su carrera desde que cumplió los 40. Entre todos los jugadores que han anotado 20 o más con 40 en la historia de la NBA, no le cazarían (67). Además, LeBron igualó a Kareem Abdul-Jabbar como el quinto jugador más veterano en la historia de la NBA (41 años y 304 días), con un partido de 20 o más. "Hitos de viejos", como dice LeBron. "Ha sido sin duda su mejor partido desde que está aquí", decía el entrenador Nick Nurse. "Al final del día, es LeBron James", destacaba Tyrese Maxey, que fue el mejor anotador de los Sixers con 27 puntos. Edgecombe hizo 13, Embiid 10 y desde el banquillo, Anfernee Simmons aportó 21 ante la baja de Jalen Brown. En los Knicks, con un balance de 2-4, Brunson se fue hasta 24 y Towns firmó 22. Nueva York hizo un esfuerzo para tratar de ganar en el tramo final pero se cruzó en el camino un LeBron James que sigue haciendo historia.

articles.title: La patada en la entrepierna de Brooks a Murray que le costó la expulsión... y quizá el partido
articles.summary: Nadie sabe si los Suns hubieran podido ganar, pero el caso es que Dillon Brooks lideraba a su equipo con 22 puntos y 9 de 12 en tiros cuando fue expulsado. Los Nuggets acabaron ganando el partido, 120-127.
articles.body: Nadie sabe si los Suns hubieran podido ganar, pero el caso es que Dillon Brooks lideraba a su equipo con 22 puntos y 9 de 12 en tiros cuando fue expulsado. Los Nuggets acabaron ganando el partido, 120-127. La jugada es en parte hilarante y en parte absurda. Proviene de la manía de los tiradores de sacar la pierna para tratar de forzar un falta en defensa. Cuando son cazados, se ganan una técnica, pero lo de Brooks fue más allá: su patada voladora la costó la expulsión. La jugada tuvo lugar a 8:05 para el final del tercer cuarto. Ya los Nuggets ganaban, 76-84, aunque Brooks estaba siendo el mejor de su equipo. El canadiense recibió un balón en la esquina, giró un par de veces sobre sí mismo hasta que encontró un pequeño hueco para tirar. Cuando estaba en el punto más alto, extendió su pierna que se estrelló en la entrepierna de Jamal Murray, que acabó en el suelo dolorido. Los árbitros, que habían señalado falta en ataque, vieron la jugada repetida y tuvieron pocas dudas: flagrante 2 y expulsión. Murray, que acabó con 39 puntos y fue crucial al final, dijo al final del partido que en ningún caso piensa que la patada fue intencionado. Señaló que él y Brooks son amigos. Al final y al cabo, son compañeros en la selección de Canadá: "No, claro que no pienso que fue intencionada" decía Murray. "Estaba lanzando a canasta, obviamente se ve que hace algo de flopping, pero no creo que tratar de patearme en la entrepierna". Brooks no es el primero que protagoniza una patada en las 'nueces' en pleno tiro. Draymond Green, por ejemplo, es un especialista en este tipo de jugadas que le han costado más de una expulsión en su carrera.

articles.standfirst: Recital de Pritchard en Boston y de Flagg e Irving en Dallas
articles.summary: Recital de Pritchard en Boston y de Flagg e Irving en Dallas
articles.body: La NBA Cup arrancó con algunas actuaciones estelares como la de Payton Pritchard en los Celtics, la de Giannis Antetokounmpo en los Heat y la combinada de Cooper Flagg y Kyrie Irving en los Mavericks. Payton Pritchard volvió a demostrar que es uno de los mejores sextos hombre de la NBA, si no el mejor. Contra los Bulls lideró a los Celtics con 30 puntos, 20 de ellos en la primera mitad. Los Celtics derrotaron a los Bulls 125-111. Jayson Tatum sumó 26 puntos para los Celtics y Paul George otros 18. El máximo anotador de los Bulls fue Caleb Wilson, con 23. El español Hugo González disputó poco más de 15 minutos, atrapó dos rebotes y robó un balón. Además de estos partidos, los Miami Heat derrotaron por 145-125 a los Indiana Pacers con un triple-doble de Giannis Antetokounmpo (31 puntos, 17 rebotes y 10 asistencias), su segunda victoria seguida tras un inicio con cuatro partidos perdidos. Los Washington Wizards confirmaron que están para competir tras el 95-79 propinado a los Charlotte Hornets, con 25 puntos de Anthony Davis, 21 de Trae Young y 17 del 'rookie', número uno del último 'draft', AJ Dybantsa. En Dallas, los Mavericks se impusieron por 116-111 a los Houston Rockets, con 35 puntos de Kyrie Irving y 33 de Cooper Flagg. Con esta derrota, los Rockets perdieron su invicto y dejaron a los Memphis Grizzlies como el único equipo en pleno de victorias. Los Detroit Pistons vencieron a los Brooklyn Nets por 94-110 y los Orlando Magic derrotaron a los Toronto Raptors por 121-116 pese a los 41 puntos de Scottie Barnes para los canadienses. Finalmente, los Minnesota Timberwolves ganaron por 127-101 a los Clippers de Los Ángeles, con cinco munutos y cero puntos de Baba Miller, mientras que los Denver Nuggets se impusieron a los Phoenix Suns a domicilio por 120 a 127.

articles.title: 1 Trade Still Haunting Every NBA Franchise In 2026
articles.summary: Ghosts are scary. Full stop.
articles.body:
But ghosts of trades past still bouncing around the nightmares of the NBA teams that brokered them? Well, that's the kind of horror befitting of the Halloween season.

Because the trade market is almost always active, it's bound to feature mistakes and the regrets that come along with them. Every franchise has them. In fact, they all have ones recent enough to still spook them.

From major, timeline-disrupting misfires to minor miscalculations of fit, readiness or value, let's take an appropriately timed stroll through the trades gone wrong (and, in a lot of cases, still going wrong) of every team in the league.

The trade: Luka Dončić for Trae Young and a first-round pick

The Hawks didn't come up totally empty here, but they missed out on the chance to roster a superstar so they could have an All-Star and a draft pick that never amounted to much (Cam Reddish).

And they should've seen this coming. Not the Reddish part, obviously, but Dončić arrived with a resume as rich as any seen in a teenaged prospect. He was already a EuroBasket champion and a EuroLeague MVP. Not to mention a big playmaker with two-steps-ahead processing speeds, and a scoring bag already bursting at the seams.

Atlanta should've recognized the sky-high ceiling attached to him—and the difference in elevation (literally and figuratively) with Young. They instead hitched their wagon to a one-way contributor who delivered just two playoff series wins over his eight-plus seasons.

The trade: Desmond Bane for two future second-round picks

Every team has some draft-night disasters hanging above its head, and if that's as bad as the trade market gets, then the franchise is mostly faring pretty well. Now, some might argue that selling Jaylen Brown for 10 cents on the dollar this summer should instead snag this spot, but that feels premature with how Paul George is playing and without knowing what the two firsts and two seconds attached to him will deliver.

For now, then, the clearest ghost haunting this group is this 2020 draft regret, which helped Boston rid itself of Enes Kanter (smart) and create flexibility later used to sign Tristan Thompson (not ideal).

Bane, the 30th pick of that draft, wasted little time proving a whole lot of clubs miscalculated his valuation. He's a career 18.3 points per game scorer and 47.3/40.5/88.9 shooter.

The trade: Keith Bogans, MarShon Brooks, Kris Humphries, Kris Joseph, Gerald Wallace, three first-round picks and a first-round pick swap for Kevin Garnett, Paul Pierce, Jason Terry, DJ White and a future second-round pick

The Nets have enough trade skeletons in their closet to populate a cemetery. Not to pile onto their misery, but let's just note two decisions that somehow weren't obvious choices here:

Sacrificing a first-round pick later spent on Damian Lillard to rent Gerald Wallace for a season-plus and giving up four players (including Jarrett Allen), three first-round picks

Four first-round pick swaps for 80 regular-season games of James Harden.

Those doesn't look great (to say the least), but this is as egregious as it gets. Or bottom-15 all-time trade , at least.

The Nets thought they were finalizing a superteam roster, but they wound up building the Celtics' championship blueprint instead. Because while Brooklyn wound up getting a single playoff series out of this exchange, Boston constructed a perennial contender (and one-time champion) by turning two of those picks into Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown.

The trade: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander for Miles Bridges and two future second-round picks

The same franchise that once drafted and traded Kobe Bryant made another franchise-altering mistake during the 2018 talent grab. The Hornets spent the No. 11 pick on Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, the two-time defending MVP and single biggest factor in the Oklahoma City Thunder's run of dominance.

But Charlotte shipped it out immediately, apparently favoring the fit of Miles Bridges over SGA alongside then-franchise face Kemba Walker. Everything about this decision quickly fell apart, including Walker's significance to the organization, as he was sign-and-traded out of Buzz City barely a year after this trade.

Bridges had some loud stat lines in Charlotte, but he was functionally a scoring specialist who wasn't particularly efficient at the craft. Those second-rounders, meanwhile, were spent on Vernon Carey Jr. and Scottie Lewis, who combined to play all of 25 games for the Hornets.

The trade: Wendell Carter Jr., Otto Porter Jr. and two first-round draft picks for Al-Farouq Aminu and Nikola Vučević

The previous Bulls regime guessed wrong on a number of topics, but they typically showcased their errors at the draft or in free agency. But this March 2021 trade, brokered with the intention of giving Zach LaVine a co-star, stands out as a pretty massive swing and a miss.

Chicago, as it would prove wont to do, overinflated its standing within the Eastern Conference and pushed a ton of chips toward a team that topped out at Play-In mediocrity. The Bulls then compounded that mistake by clinging to that core for way too long and torpedoing the returns from its inevitable sell-off.

The process was flawed from the start, but it grew worse with time. Both picks landed in the lottery, and while Orlando only connected on one, it was a pretty massive get (Franz Wagner, No. 8 in 2021). It also found a new interior anchor in Carter, who's been a mostly locked-in starter and nightly double-double threat ever since.

The trade: Ricky Rubio, a lottery-protected first-round pick and two second-round picks for Caris LeVert

To be transparent here, there was non-zero consideration given to last season's deadline deal swapping out Darius Garland for James Harden. That was (and is) risky given their respective ages and Harden's shaky track record, but since Donovan Mitchell signed off on it , it's probably reasonable to assume that helped secure his long-term commitment .

So, let's time travel back to his 2022 trade deadline deal, when the Cavs sought out perimeter depth and secondary scoring and creation from LeVert. It was a reasonable enough wager, and you could argue LeVert lived up to his end of the deal across parts of four seasons in Northeast Ohio.

His play style wasn't super compatible with Donovan Mitchell and Darius Garland, though, and the price wound up being higher in hindsight. Because one of those second-round picks became Andrew Nembhard, a two-way contributor and rock-solid starter, and the first landed Ben Sheppard, a 6'6" guard with encouraging three-and-D flashes.

The trade: Luka Dončić, Maxi Kleber and Markieff Morris for Max Christie, Anthony Davis and a 2029 first-round pick

Look, that sounds hyperbolic, but we did run the numbers, and...yeah. Yikes.

Dončić is a once-in-a-lifetime type of megatalent. Davis is older, more injury-prone and far less dynamic on the defensive end. A healthy version of Davis might help complete a puzzle, but Dončić can almost paint the picture himself.

Nothing about this deal made sense. Dallas' willingness to deal Dončić was a head-scratcher on its own, but this went from bad business to a fireable offense (in the same calendar year ) when the Mavericks muted their own market by negotiating with only a single suitor .

While the Lakers have reconfigured their roster around Dončić, the Mavericks have already moved on from Davis (and the executive who brokered this blockbuster). Oh, and that 2029 first-round pick probably won't be great, since Dallas brightened L.A.'s future by gifting it Luka freakin' Dončić.

The trade: Michael Porter Jr. and an unprotected future first-round pick for Cameron Johnson

Admittedly, the Nuggets have more glaring misfires on their resume. They drafted both Rudy Gobert and Donovan Mitchell and didn't nab even a short-term keeper in either exchange. Those are arguably worse trade crimes, but they're also distant memories, and they're filled with enough what-if variables that they might not haunt anyone outside of the history books.

This deal is different. It only went down in July 2025, so the wound is still fresh enough to feel it. And, yes, it is very much a wound, even if the Nuggets felt they needed to do this in order to dial back some of their spending.

You know what's not a great look, though? Having a contending-caliber roster built around the planet's best player (Nikola Jokić) and then doing a deal in which you're sending out the better player and the only pick involved (an unprotected future first at that). Porter has said the Nuggets got this wrong, and this is our agreement.

The trade: Jaden Ivey and cash for Kevin Huerter and a first-round pick swap

In terms of trade value, this is fine. In fact, it's probably better than fine, since Ivey is out of the league, Huerter is in Detroit's rotation and the first-round swap later helped the Pistons swing a trade for intriguing rookie Ebuka Okorie.

So, what's the problem? Well, Ivey seemed at least asset-adjacent at the time of this trade, a great change-of-scenery candidate who seemed he might thrive in a system with more on-ball opportunities. And Detroit's payroll flexibility made it the rare contending team with the ability to add salary.

So, the Pistons had a chance to strike and tried to capitalize on it—but they splurged on the wrong player. Huerter is a shooting specialist who hasn't actually been even a league-average shooter for a while now. In fact, he's toting around an unsightly sub-30 percent connection rate during his 30-game tenure with the team so far.

The trade: Jonathan Kuminga and Buddy Hield for Kristaps Porziņģis

Because the Warriors dragged out Kuminga's clearly inevitable departure for so long, they really wrecked the kind of return they could expect to fetch. That said, they didn't totally tank it, so they should have found something in return for the athletic swingman.

Instead they rolled the dice on Porziņģis, an oft-injured big man who was struggling to get control of a health situation even before he arrived. That health situation has since become career-threatening , and even if he's able to suit up again, it sounds like that won't happen in Golden State.

"Team sources continue to express an extreme level of pessimism that Porzingis will ever play for the Warriors again," ESPN's Anthony Slater reported.

The Warriors, who are already missing both Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody, now have a $20 million player absent from the equation. They're also noticeably lacking size, spacing, paint protection and support scoring—all boxes Porziņģis was intended to check.

The trade: Chris Paul, two first-round picks and two first-round pick swaps to the Oklahoma City Thunder for Russell Westbrook

This July 2019 trade was supposed to give Houston one last shot at extending the James Harden era and helping him get over the championship hump. It wound up closing that chapter for good instead.

While Harden and Westbrook shared a hoops history, there was also an oil-and-water element to their stylistic fit. Harden needed a knockdown shooter who was comfortable playing off the ball; Westbrook was one of the more ball-dominant players of his generation and one of the least reliable volume shooters this league has ever seen.

The Rockets won a playoff series that season, but that was it. Westbrook, Daryl Morey and Mike D'Antoni were all out of Space City that summer, and Harden forced his way out during the early portion of the following season. While the draft swaps never conveyed, the picks themselves became a couple of intriguing guard prospects in Nikola Topić and Labaron Philon Jr.

The trade: Isaiah Jackson, Bennedict Mathurin, two first-round picks and a second-round pick for Ivica Zubac and Kobe Brown

Pacers fans (and probably front office members) will side-eye this selection, and they have every right to. It's way too early to tell what kind of career Zubac will have in Indiana, and his on-paper fit with this group remains strong.

So, "haunt" might feel a bit harsh, but here's why it could still work. A few months after making this deal, Pacers president of basketball operations Kevin Pritchard felt the need to apologize for it, as the top-four protected pick sacrificed in this deal came in at No. 5 and therefore conveyed to the Clippers:

Would it have been impossible for Indy to do this deal with top-five protection instead of top-four? That was surely discussed, but even so, it seems like the kind of question that could contribute to a lot of sleepless nights in the Circle City—especially if Keaton Wagler, the player taken fifth overall, starts tapping more into his star potential.

The trade: Danilo Gallinari, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, five first-round picks and two first-round pick swaps for Paul George

Clippers fans will try to justify some of this cost by noting that this deal was required to gain Kawhi Leonard's commitment. They'll also note that, at the time, expectations were enormous for the George-Leonard pairing, and that no one really knew what kind of player Gilgeous-Alexander, fresh off a solid but unspectacular rookie season, would become.

All of that is fine, and all of that is true. This is still a yikes. Just the George-for-SGA elements looks atrocious in hindsight, and that's before factoring in how some of these draft picks became Jalen Williams, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Aday Mara.

So, what did L.A. collect for such an astronomic cost? Three series wins across five seasons with the George-Leonard partnership in place and now the bleakest future in basketball . Say it with me, folks: YIKES!

The trade: Ivica Zubac and Michael Beasley for Mike Muscala

Remember how the Lakers, prior this summer, had a glaring hole at the center position? You know, the one they sacrificed two unprotected firsts, two unprotected swaps and $130 million for Walker Kessler to cover up this offseason?

Well, it never needed to exist. The Lakers had a fully capable center in place long before this, but they didn't give Zubac the chance to earn the role (despite strong per-36-minutes numbers suggesting he clearly deserved an audition). Instead, they included him in a laughably bad offer to rent Muscala for the latter portion of a non-playoff season.

Muscala bolted in free agency right after and bounced around a few franchises before calling it quits in 2024. Zubac, on the other hand, established himself as a legitimate starter shortly thereafter and routinely ranks favorably among the Association's non-star centers.

The trade: Trey Murphy III, Jonas Valančiūnas, Brandon Boston Jr. and Tyler Harvey for Ziaire Williams, Steven Adams, Eric Bledsoe, Jared Butler and two future second-round picks

Hoops historians, who might be a little hazy on the particulars, might wonder why the Grizzlies got so little in return for Ja Morant this summer. Because if he stays upright and on the attack, he's a steal for the paltry price Portland paid (Jerami Grant and Kris Murray).

This close to the trade, though, it's easy to remember how much a split seemed needed for all parties involved and how much damage Morant's availability issues had done to his market value. The Grizzlies probably got what they could.

A much more haunting memory, then, is this 2021 attempt by Memphis to plug up a problematic hole on the wing. The Grizzlies made an aggressive move up for Williams, the 10th pick, not knowing they could have had the actual solution at their original selection spot with Murphy, the 17th pick.

The trade: Kyle Lowry and a future first-round pick for Terry Rozier

Was there some temptation to go with the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade? Sadly, yes—and not for engagement purposes. He has been exactly as advertised, and you'd much rather have a superstar player than not, but this feels like the textbook reason why teams can't get themselves in this kind of pursuit. It's a win-right-away attempt, but Miami didn't leave enough pieces in place to allow Antetokounmpo to lead a winner.

The Heat aren't feeling buyer's remorse or anything, but they are surely struggling to identify means of fleshing out the roster around him.

But this Jan. 2024 trade for Rozier? It's just all regret, and that can be said while keeping the focus entirely on the (basketball) court. Rozier was either injured or ineffective over the past season-plus, and Miami doesn't even know how much he actually cost. The draft pick carries lottery protection in 2027, but if it's not conveyed, the safety net evaporates, and it'll be an unprotected 2028 first. Gulp .

The trade: Jrue Holiday, a first-round pick and two first-round pick swaps for Damian Lillard

Franchises can (relatively) easily get over a mistake that was just a miscalculation from the start. They'll wonder what the heck they were thinking, obviously, but they can own the error and move on.

This trade was different. This was supposed to work. Milwaukee needed a move capable of convincing Giannis Antetokounmpo to stick around , and this felt like it could scratch that itch and do so much more. Lillard had ample star power of his own, and his imaginary connection with Antetokounmpo on pick-and-roll plays felt unguardable.

But that never became reality. Lillard and Antetokounmpo had great individual moments, but their whole fell short of the sum of their parts. The injury bug got the better of both, too, limiting this partnership to three playoff wins (games, not series) over two seasons before the Bucks waived and stretched Lillard's remaining salary to sign Myles Turner to an over-market deal.

The trade: A first-round pick and a first-round pick swap for Rob Dillingham

This haunt lands under the right-idea, wrong-execution label. Had the 2024 draft deal worked, the Wolves would've had a successor for Mike Conley, scoring and creation help for Anthony Edwards and some cost-controlled relief for their climbing payroll costs.

So, again, the logic was there; Minnesota just erred on the target. Dillingham wasn't remotely worth the cost. A lack of size (6'2", 175 lbs.) forced him to wrestle with a steep learning curve, and the win-now Wolves, conference finalists the previous season, could ill-afford to stomach his growing pains.

Dillingham didn't exactly force the issue, though, struggling with everything from shooting and creating to playmaking and defending. The Wolves abandoned hope by the 2026 trade deadline, and Dillingham, who was traded again in September, isn't even on an NBA roster now.

The trade: Asa Newell and a first-round pick for Derik Queen

Had the Pelicans gotten luckier (or maybe unluckier would be the better way to phrase it) at the 2026 lottery, this haunt could've been nightmarish. Because the draft pick used to move up for Queen was the better of theirs or the Bucks', meaning it had serious helium in a celebrated draft class.

The pick wound up landing eighth overall, leaving it clear of the super-elite class at the top, though still delivering a possible star (Kingston Flemings). So, it certainly could've been worse.

That doesn't really erase the bad-business regret of it all, though. It's too early to make major proclamations about the kind of career Queen will or won't have, but his questionable (at best) fit with Zion Williamson was clear from the start. If New Orleans was fully committed to a youth movement, maybe that wouldn't matter, but the Pels keep stiff-arming trade suitors who come calling about their plug-and-play vets.

The trade: Five first-round picks and a first-round pick swap for Mikal Bridges

The Knicks brokered this trade—which featured other moving parts, but these were the ones that mattered—in July 2024, plugged Bridges into their starting five and celebrated a title less than two years later. The defending champs might laugh at the notion they are haunted by anything at the moment.

But with New York grappling with a sky-high payroll and struggling to relieve it without losing a key contributor due to their asset shortage, doesn't this deal feel like the direct precursor to those problems? Bridges peaked as a solid starter, and he has struggled to even live up to that label here lately.

The Knicks, though, paid a megastar trade price to get him, and the total tally won't be clear for a while, since they're still on the hook for unprotected first-round picks in 2027, 2029 and 2031 (plus an unprotected 2028 swap). Bridges, who's off to a dreadful start this season, has averaged 15.7 points, 3.7 assists and 3.4 rebounds over 169 games in New York.

The trade: Alperen Şengün for two first-round picks

The Thunder failed to defend their title last season in part because they struggled to find an offensive co-star for Shai Gilgeous-Alexander amid Jalen Williams' injury issues. With Williams now shelved by a devastating leg injury, OKC might have to hit the trade market for offensive reinforcements.

You know what the Thunder are unlikely to find there? A two-time All-Star, 24-year-old center who might be taking his game to previously unseen heights. And that hurts because Şengün was originally drafted by them, only to be quickly rerouted to the Rockets for draft assets the Thunder later used as part of a package for Ousmane Dieng, who was salary dumped at last season's deadline.

Şengün is now an offensive hub for a Houston team that appears ready to challenge the very best in the West—OKC included. His 24.5 points and 7.0 assists are both career-highs, as are each layer of his sizzling 58.1/66.7/76.9 shooting slash.

The trade: Four first-round picks, one first-round pick swap, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Cole Anthony for Desmond Bane

This feels a little icky to list here, since Bane has been mostly solid for the Magic (and helpful in the ways they needed him to be), and it's never easy criticizing a club for trying to for it.

But Orlando made this aggressive June 2025 move under the assumption it was a Desmond Bane away from a championship breakthrough. That's the only way to justify forking over this many assets for a zero-time All-Star.

The Magic just weren't as close as they thought. They also haven't seen the kind of superstar growth they seemingly projected for Paolo Banchero, as neither he nor Franz Wagner feels at all capable of steering a championship run. They were 41-win, first-round losers the season before Bane's arrival and 45-win, first-round losers during his first go-round with the group.

The trade: Jayson Tatum and a future first-round pick for Markelle Fultz

The Sixers might have processed their way into Joel Embiid, but their other maneuvers atop the draft board were almost all misfires. None was more punishing than this seemingly simple swap ahead of the 2017 draft, which saw Philly flip the No. 3 pick and a future first (later used on Romeo Langford) for the No. 1 pick.

It was bold, it was daring and it was wholly unnecessary. Had Boston stayed at No. 1, it was planning to take Tatum anyway. At least, that's his word and the team's .

Shoulder issues short-circuited Fultz's shooting mechanics, and his NBA film never came close to what his college work said it would be. He was in and out of Philly in fewer than two seasons, and he last held an NBA roster spot in March. Tatum, of course, has ascended to superstar status, earning six All-Star selections and four All-NBA first-team honors (and counting) while piloting a championship run.

The trade: A future first-round pick, Grayson Allen and Royce O'Neale for Miles Bridges, a second-round pick and a protected first-round pick

Too soon? Some will certainly say that, since Bridges has only made three appearances since the Suns added him in July. That side loses a lot of steam, though, when you consider this looked like a bad, overpriced trade from the start.

With Phoenix already operating at a severe asset shortage and needing to strengthen its roster around Devin Booker, it should have treated that 2033 unprotected first as its one golden ticket. But it rushed to cash it in on the decidedly average Bridges, who does nothing to improve this team's limitations with spacing, creating, and organizing.

The Suns' roster issues are real and far less easily solved after this deal. You could argue Phoenix would've been better off with Allen's shooting over Bridges' inside-the-arc scoring, making the pick portion of this trade scarier than anything you'll see in a horror movie.

The trade: Cedric Coward for Yang Hansen, a future first-round pick and two second-round picks

The Blazers haven't had many trade flops in recent memory. Not that this trade looks good or defensible, but highlighting it has some rush-to-judgment aspects, since they haven't collected those draft picks or really given Hansen his sink-or-swim chance yet.

But is anyone holding out hope that Portland will come out ahead? Because while Hansen is once again failing to secure a rotation spot, Coward is starting (and sometimes starring) for a Grizzlies team following the lead of its young core to a 5-0 start.

Coward projects as sort of a turbo-charged three-and-D wing. He can ace both of those roles, but he might add more to the equation with his attacking, finishing and gear-turning passing.

The trade: Tyrese Haliburton, Buddy Hield and Tristan Thompson for Domantas Sabonis, Justin Holiday, Jeremy Lamb and a second-round pick

Sabonis has played plenty of productive games in Sacramento since this Feb. 2022 deal went down. Very few of them have carried any kind of significance, and the biggest development in Sacramento now is when it can find a taker for Sabonis and Zach LaVine and lean fully into a youth movement.

The Kings just misjudged a few things with this trade. Like the height of Haliburton's ceiling. Or the amount of time they could keep De'Aaron Fox content. And the specific challenges of building a winner around Sabonis given his unique strengths and weaknesses.

The Kings have no identity and no real hope for the foreseeable future beyond whatever mileage they think they can get out of Darius Acuff Jr.'s volume production. The Pacers, meanwhile, know exactly how they want to play and how good they can be, having already had an NBA Finals run orchestrated by Haliburton.

The trade: Kawhi Leonard for DeMar DeRozan, Jakob Poeltl and a first-round pick

The Spurs don't exactly make many missteps, so we have to hit the wayback machine and revisit this July 2018 decision. It may, however, have some new haunts this summer, since Leonard was involved in a trade that arguably delivered a better return—Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two unprotected future firsts, a first-round swap and two seconds—despite Leonard being older, more injury-prone and in the middle of a salary cap circumvention investigation.

There were, of course, factors working against San Antonio at the time. Everyone knew Leonard wanted out . He was coming off an injury-ravaged nine-game season and approaching the final year on his contract.

Even still, that's a pretty nothing return for a star two-way wing in the heart of his prime. And it was clearly shortsighted, with the Spurs (for some reason) seeking immediate competitiveness over long-term assets. San Antonio lost in the first round the following season and started a long playoff drought right after, while Toronto, of course, won it all in Leonard's first (and, at the time, only) season.

The trade: A first-round pick, two second-round picks and Khem Birch for Jakob Poeltl

The value doesn't seem atrocious here, especially since the first-round pick wound up being draft bust Rob Dillingham. Still, it was a healthy investment in a center who ranked somewhere between fine and pretty good.

It also started a pattern of the Raptors investing too much into Poeltl, which now stands as perhaps the biggest hurdle on their road to contention.

Because they didn't just stop at this deal. They doubled-down on that commitment by giving him a four-year, $104 million extension that just kicked in this season. Back problems have plagued his availability and general abilities, rendering him a problem both on the court and on the cap sheet.

The trade: John Collins for Kyle Anderson, Kevin Love, a future second-round pick and cash

The Jazz have generally done well when they have dabbled in the trade market. Depending on how things go, maybe the aggressive move for Jaren Jackson Jr. will challenge that notion, but they need more time to shift their mindset and get healthy before that 2026 deadline deal can be properly evaluated.

So, let's instead revisit this July 2025 trade, even if the players involved aren't the kind to keep anyone up at night. The Jazz were clearing out money and clearing up minutes for their young players, and this trade helped on both fronts.

It just feels like there should've been more available for Collins. He was super productive the season prior (19 points on 52.7/39.9/84.8 shooting, 8.2 rebounds in 30.5 minutes) and shined bright enough as a play-finisher for the Pistons to make him a part of their championship-hopeful plan this past summer.

The trade: Kristaps Porziņģis for Tyus Jones, Danilo Gallinari, Mike Muscala and Julian Phillips

The Wizards are one of the true wait-and-see teams of this entire exercise. Because trading for and then maxing out Trae Young certainly feels like a temptation of fate, and the same would ring true if they give Anthony Davis the kind of coin he's seeking .

That said, the trade costs for both were entirely reasonable, and they are legitimate need-fillers when healthy. Washington can also balance some overpays (to a degree) with a wealth of rookie-scale contracts on the books.

So, we'll spare those trades of haunting status for now and instead spotlight this June 2023 exchange. Porziņģis should've had real trade value then, as he'd just filled the shot-blocking, floor-spacing unicorn mold while also serving as a 23.2-points-per-game scorer across 65 contests. But the Wizards turned him into almost nothing, as Phillips was rerouted immediately, and Jones, Gallinari and Muscala were all out of Washington by the following summer.

articles.title: La lesión de Chet Holmgren abre la puerta de la titularidad a Aday Mara
articles.standfirst: Holmgren es el tercer titular que pierden los Thunder en apenas cinco partidos
articles.summary: Holmgren es el tercer titular que pierden los Thunder en apenas cinco partidos
articles.body: Lo de los Thunder empieza a ser una maldición. Nunca en la NBA, un equipo calificado como claro favorito al título, había sido tan golpeado por las lesiones en el arranque de la temporada como la franquicia de Oklahoma. El último en caer ha sido Chet Holmgren. Según anunció su equipo, Holmgren estará al menos entre ocho y 10 semanas de baja por culpa de un desgarro del tendón rotuliano en su rodilla derecha. Habrá que ver cómo marcha a recuperación y si el jugador no necesita más tiempo de descanso. La noticia, para el equipo que en mayo debería estar jugándose un billete para las Finales con los Spurs, no dejaría de ser un contratiempo sino fuera porque Holmgren es el tercer titular que cae con una lesión de larga duración. En un mismo partido, los Thunder perdieron a Jalen Williams (fractura de fíbula y tobillo dislocado) y Cason Wallace (fractura del labrum), para el resto de la temporada. En cualquier otro equipo este drama sería devastador. A los Thunder les toca reinventarse. Ya lo están haciendo. Del cinco titular de los tres primeros partidos y que iba a ser la tónica toda la temporada formado por Gilgeous-Alexander, Wallace, Williams, Holmgren y Hartenstein, el paisaje ha dibujado otro con Shai y Hartenstein, pero con Jared McCain, Ajay Mitchell y Kenrich Williams, en los últimos dos. Parece claro que, al margen de los fichajes y refuerzos que hagan los Thunder, como el de Ochai Agbaji para mejorar la rotación, los jóvenes y menos habituales tendrán que dar un paso adelante. Y ahí entra en acción Aday Mara. El zaragozano ha jugado en los cinco partidos de los Thunder, aunque ninguno como titular. Promedia 15,8 minutos contra los 23,8 de Hartenstein o los 30 de Holmgren. Mara verá aumentado su tiempo en pista en el próximo mes y medio. Pero también se abre una oportunidad para poder vivir sus primeros minutos como titular. Mara no era el sustituto directo de Holmgren, que es más un ala-pívot, sino de Hartenstein. Pero Mark Daigneault podría estudiar la opción de que Mara y Hartenstein convivan más tiempo juntos en pista y que incluso lleguen a comenzar un partido. Ante los Suns Mara firmó su primer doble-doble con 11 puntos y 10 rebotes en 20 minutos y su capacidad para poner tapones y alterar tiros y jugadas es una mina de oro para la defensa de Oklahoma. Eso sí, perdería amenaza de tiro exterior, ya que entre los dos jugadores llevan un 0/1 en triples en cinco partidos (el único fue un intento de Mara que no entró), mientras que Holmgren en tres partidos ha hecho un 2/6 y es un jugador con un 36,8% de acierto desde el triple. Hay que tener en cuenta que estas tres lesiones, sobre todo las de Williams y Wallace, son de especial dramatismo teniendo en cuenta que los Thunder perdieron potencial en su rotación en verano cuando decidieron traspasar a Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins e Isaiah Joe por razones económicas (límite salarial). De esa forma, los Thunder (4-1 en su balance), afrontan semanas de incertidumbre en su juego y pueden encontrar en Aday Mara una enorme solución tanto para iniciar los partidos como para jugar muchos minutos.

articles.title: Arizona Wildcats look to pull off upset of No 13 Texas Tech in pivotal Big 12 football showdown
articles.summary: No. 22 Arizona takes on No. 13 Texas Tech in a college football Big 12 showdown with playoff implications and Noah Fifita leading the Wildcats.
articles.body: College Football brings us another great slate of football games on Saturday. The past few weeks have been full of upsets and wild games. It seems like no one can keep hold of the top few spots in the rankings this year. That provides a much more enjoyable watch than chalky outcomes. After all, we are watching kids play a sport, and most won’t continue on to play professionally. One of the two matches between ranked teams happens today, so we know both of them will move up or down the Top-25 list after this, with Arizona taking on Texas Tech. Arizona comes into the game with a 6-1 record and a 3-1 mark in the Big 12. They are ranked 22nd in the nation. The Wildcats started their season with a win over Northern Arizona. Then in Week 2, they had to face BYU, and we’ve seen the Cougars be one of the best teams in the country. Arizona lost this game 28-17. Since that loss, they’ve run off five straight wins over Northern Illinois, Washington State, Cincinnati, West Virginia, and Iowa State. The Wildcats really haven’t had a tough game outside of the matchup with BYU. They only have two other ranked teams on the schedule – today against Texas Tech, and in a few weeks against Utah. If they can win both of those games, they have at least a legitimate shot to win the Big 12, and they could even find their way into the College Football Playoffs. He hasn’t gotten a ton of attention in the Heisman talk, but Noah Fifita has been fantastic for the team. Fifita is completing 75% of passes, has 18 touchdowns, and four interceptions. WEEK 7 AP TOP 25 POLL FEATURES A COMPLETE SHUFFLE AFTER CHAOTIC WEEKEND, WITH MIAMI TAKING OVER THE TOP SPOT Texas Tech is currently ranked 13th in the nation, and they are 6-1 for the year as well. They also have a 3-1 record in Big 12 play. Their lone loss of the season came last week in shocking fashion to Cincinnati. It wasn’t particularly close, either. They went on the road, and they dropped the game to the Bearcats 37-24. The biggest issue in this game was probably the turnovers from Texas Tech. They threw an interception and had two fumbles lost. It didn’t help that the Bearcats scored 24 points in the 2nd quarter of the game, and all of them within the last eight minutes of the half. Texas Tech had been rolling before last week. They won the first six games of the season. In the first game, they beat Abilene Christian by 23. In Week 2, they were able to top Oregon State by 11 points. In Week 3, they had their first test, and that was a battle against Houston. In that game, they won 28-26, but clearly it was a close battle. The next three games were fairly easy matchups with Sam Houston, Colorado, and Arizona State all not putting up much of a fight against the Red Raiders. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP This afternoon’s game is a battle between two Big 12 beasts. The Wildcats have a legitimate shot at pulling off the upset. I really like the way that Fifita has played and positioned his squad for wins. Texas Tech’s defense has been a big piece of their game, and I’ve been pretty unimpressed with their offense. I think these two teams are fairly evenly matched. I know Texas Tech will be looking for revenge or to bounce back. I’m going to take the Wildcats with the points, though. I think they have the right offense to battle against Texas Tech. Give me Arizona +3.5. For more sports betting information and plays, follow David on X/Twitter: @futureprez2024

articles.title: El Movistar Estudiantes se mide al Gran Canaria en la 'primera final' por el ascenso
articles.standfirst: Ambos equipos son los grandes favoritos en la Primera FEB para ascender a la Liga Endesa
articles.summary: Ambos equipos son los grandes favoritos en la Primera FEB para ascender a la Liga Endesa
articles.body: Hay partidos que trascienden la clasificación y que evocan tiempos en los que los grandes duelos del baloncesto español tenían en el Movistar Estudiantes a uno de sus protagonistas habituales. El enfrentamiento de este domingo ante el Cajasiete Gran Canaria (18:30 horas) pertenece a esa categoría. Dos históricos del baloncesto nacional, dos proyectos construidos para regresar a la Liga Endesa y una primera batalla de altos vuelos en la sexta jornada de Primera FEB. El conjunto colegial llega invicto, con cinco victorias en cinco encuentros, pero enfrente tendrá a uno de los grandes aspirantes al ascenso y un rival que conoce bien las exigencias de la máxima categoría. El Gran Canaria, recién descendido después de 31 temporadas consecutivas en la ACB, no ha aterrizado en la segunda categoría para quedarse. Con Bruno Savignani al frente, los insulares han reunido una plantilla de garantías, con nombres como Carlos Alocén, Joe Cremo, Luke Fischer, Marques Townes y Fran Guerra. Este último, formado en la cantera estudiantil, será uno de los principales peligros para los de Toni Ten. No será el único reencuentro: Christian Díaz, Joaquín Rodríguez, Juan Rubio y Roberts Stumbris también cuentan con pasado colegial. Una buena parte de la historia reciente del Estu estará, por tanto, en el bando contrario. El partido también enfrenta a dos entrenadores con credenciales para aspirar a todo. Ten, que la pasada temporada se quedó a las puertas del ascenso tras perder la final ante el Leyma Coruña en la prórroga, busca completar el trabajo iniciado hace un año. Savignani, por su parte, llega avalado por su trayectoria en la categoría y por haber conseguido el ascenso con el Burgos. Dos técnicos que comparten una apuesta por la identidad colectiva, el esfuerzo y la competitividad. Sobre la pista, buena parte de los focos estarán puestos en el duelo exterior entre Omar Silverio, máximo anotador estudiantil con 14 puntos de media, y Marques Townes, uno de los principales argumentos ofensivos del conjunto canario. Pero hay otro factor que puede resultar determinante: la grada. El Estudiantes quiere recuperar aquellas tardes en las que el Palacio se convertía en una de las canchas más intimidatorias del baloncesto español, cuando el empuje de la Demencia y el resto de la afición convertían cada partido importante en una experiencia difícil de olvidar. El club necesita que el Movistar Arena vuelva a respirar ese ambiente, que la gente acuda y que el equipo sienta el respaldo de una afición que parece estar recuperando la conexión con sus jugadores. Toni Ten percibió algo especial en el último encuentro disputado en casa. "En la segunda parte yo noté cosas y sentí cosas, y creo que el equipo también. Lo hablábamos en el vestuario, que hasta ahora no habíamos sentido y notado", reconocía el técnico, que quiere alimentar esa complicidad. "Nosotros tenemos que ayudar desde la pista, dando razones para ello. Creo que es un equipo que pone esfuerzo, energía y carácter, pero con la ayuda de la grada nos multiplicamos", explicaba. El entrenador colegial incluso puso palabras a una sensación que quiere convertir en habitual: "Entre todos habíamos generado una atmósfera en la que nos sentíamos indestructibles, en la que nos sentíamos imparables. Esa sensación de que somos imparables, somos indestructibles. Y la generamos nosotros y la ha generado esta arena". Un mensaje que conecta con el lema de esta temporada y con la necesidad de que el Movistar Arena vuelva a ser un fortín. "Eso es muy bonito, que pase eso, deberíamos conseguirlo", insistía. La jornada tendrá además un componente solidario. Movistar Estudiantes regalará una entrada para el encuentro a todas las personas que hayan donado sangre desde el 28 de octubre y puedan acreditarlo, en reconocimiento a quienes están colaborando tras el accidente ferroviario. Los justificantes podrán presentarse en las taquillas del pabellón desde una hora y media antes del inicio del partido. La clasificación todavía no dicta sentencias y el resultado no será definitivo en la carrera por el ascenso, pero sí servirá para medir las aspiraciones de dos candidatos. El Estudiantes quiere seguir invicto y mandar un mensaje a sus rivales. Para ello necesitará baloncesto, carácter y, sobre todo, recuperar ese rugido colectivo que convirtió sus grandes noches en recuerdos imborrables.
